authorship: No authorship of this argument or source records by this reviewer
reasoning: A rational nonconstant function on a principal open has a real ball avoiding its denominator. Density of rational points, closedness of Z and connectedness force a polynomial identity if its rational values were all integral. Dominant unirational parametrization preserves nonconstancy.

For degree<=2, three distinct input values give a line with identically zero restriction or a rational plane conic. Reducible plane restrictions contain a line with nonconstant input; an irreducible quadratic has a smooth rational point among the three. Every branch contradicts the rational-function lemma. Finite factor unions exclude reducible cubics.

A rationally irreducible geometrically reducible cubic has three distinct conjugate linear factors. Rational zeros at inputs0 and1 lie on all three hyperplanes; their joining line gives every rational input.

For a geometrically integral cubic, quotient by the full rational kernel of directional derivatives removes all geometric vertex directions because kernel formation commutes with field extension. Translation at inputs0 and1 forces both input linear forms to kill the vertex. A rational section therefore preserves the entire input projection.

In dimension>=2 the quotient meets the retained final1989 CTS proposition: characteristic zero, geometrically integral, noncone and a rational point. Singular points are permitted by that source. Its unirationality contradicts the nonconstant input.

The plane-curve branch uses integral HIT, not rational specialization. The accepted final Müller introduction supplies infinitely many integer specializations over Q; deleting leading-coefficient/denominator zeros retains irreducibility and degree>=2, hence no rational root. Degree0/1 and dimension0 branches are handled separately.
scope: Full current elementary argument and exact use of retained CTS/integral-HIT sources. Source papers are reused through pinned independent source acceptances, not freshly audited in this receipt. Does not on its own prove the degree-four upper bound or whole integer-definition theorem.
